lines.note: Saikai is glossed by nishi no umi, the western sea. The initial entry also explains the preceding page's Sai- catchword without expanding it there.

runs.text: Caminho, ou eſtrada do Miaco pe-

lines.note: Saikaidoo names the road from Miaco toward the west. The headword's long o has a downward caron; the Portuguese pera is divided at the edge.
This completes the route's direction, toward the western regions, and the divided pera from the preceding row.
Saicaixi and Saicaxi are alternative names for a tree. The upright l introduces the alternative; its useful fruit is described next.

runs.text: que dà hũa fruita boa pera mezinha.

lines.note: The tree bears fruit considered useful as medicine. Printed dà and hũa retain their grave and tilde; fruita and mezinha are not modernized.
Saikan denotes resourcefulness and diligence. The scan restores the missing i in Saican and reads Induſtria, not Indaſtria.
Saikanna describes a diligent, resourceful person, the adjectival counterpart of the preceding noun.
Saikanni is explicitly marked as an adverb, inheriting the sense of acting diligently or resourcefully from the preceding entries.
This is a cross-reference from the alternative tree name Saicaxi to Saicaixi, not a new botanical description. The target remains upright.
Saichi denotes ingenuity and knowledge. The Portuguese gloss separates resourcefulness from learning while keeping both senses together.
Saichuu is the midst or height of something. Printed Monaca is retained as the Japanese gloss; it is not silently normalized to a more expected modern form.
Kassen no saichuu ni gives the first example, in the midst of battle. The printed division No- continues into meo on the next row.
The battle example is translated as its midst and fervour; gakumon no then begins the corresponding example about study. Its terminal hyphen is visible.
The study example means being in the midst or intensity of study. Fu begins fuyu, winter, below; no hyphen is added where none is printed.
Fuyu no saichuu is the heart of winter. This completes the divided Japanese word and the sequence of examples for saichuu.
Saikoo, explained by futatabi okosu, means building or raising again. The circumflex over o is retained rather than assimilated to the carons nearby.

runs.text: tornar aleuãtar algũa couſa que eſtaua ja caida,

lines.note: The object is something already fallen that is raised again. The abbreviation tilde in aleuãtar and the printed algũa remain unexpanded.
The object may also have been ruined. Iye wo saikoo suru illustrates rebuilding a house; desbaratada keeps the supplied short s.

runs.text: nar a edificar, ou aleuantar caſa.

lines.note: The example is translated as building or raising a house again, completing Tornar from the preceding physical row.

Saikoku is glossed as nishi no kuni, the western countries or realms. The final i is upright in the scan; it introduces the following specification of the region rather than forming part of the italic definition.

runs.text: Eſtes noue reinos deſta ilha do Ximo.

lines.note: The explanation identifies nine realms of the island called Ximo, then begins Qiuu-shuu. Ximo occurs within Portuguese prose, unlike the Japanese synonym that follows.

Xuu completes Qiuu-shuu, followed by the alternative Chikushi. At far right, the separately placed (genhoſo de mãos. completes en- in the Saicu entry below, not this geographical entry. Its omitted de mãos. and exceptional placement are restored while preserving physical order.
Saiku is explained by komakani takumu, fine craftsmanship. The Portuguese means an artisan or someone dexterous with the hands; en- continues in the displaced far-right fragment on the preceding row.

runs.text: Faca de que vſa o official. l,

lines.note: Saiku gatana is the knife used by a craftsman. The scan reads Saicu, not Saica, and official, not the draft's separated and malformed o fficiat.
This alternative description means someone dexterous with the hands, completing the knife entry's account of its user. The supplied tilde position in maõs is retained.

runs.text: Official mecanico, ou engenhoſo de mãos.

lines.note: Saikunin denotes a manual craftsman or skilled artisan. The scan supports double f in Official and final o in engenhoſo rather than the draft's feminine ending.
Saidai, glossed by mottomo ookinari, means very great or large. The abbreviation tilde in grã- is retained across the Portuguese line break.
This finishes grande, very large. The upright S. marks written usage rather than belonging to the italic definition.
Saidaiji names certain red medicinal pellets or prepared grains. The scan reads confeiçoens with f, distinguishing preparations from the draft's misleading long-s reading.
The preparations are said to be used for various illnesses. The close-set variasdoenças is retained as in the supplied transcription, without adding a modern word break.
Saidan is explained as discussing again, futatabi danzuru. The Portuguese gives consultation or conference before adding the repetition sense below.
This completes the alternative meaning, repetition of something. The printed tilde in algũa remains on u.
Saido means saving, explained by sukui tasukuru. Fi- begins hito, the people saved in the following example.
Hito wo saido suru means saving people. The divided word is completed without replacing the historical Japanese forms with modern equivalents.
Saido riyaku denotes salvation. The following example begins a phrase about the benefit of salvation or redemption.
Go-on completes the Japanese phrase for the benefit or grace of salvation. The Portuguese redẽpção retains its abbreviation tilde rather than expanding the missing nasal letter.
Saihai is explained as worshipping twice, futatabi ogamu. The abraded joined arches are read as m in vogamu rather than the draft's in sequence; the worship gloss supports that chosen reading.
Saihen, futatabi kayesu, means sending something again or returning it. The Portuguese amandar remains close-set as printed in the draft.
The definition finishes sending the thing again. The cup-passing example then begins, with saifen divided across the line.
The cup has already gone round a second time. Sacazuqui is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese translation; the example's Sacazzuqi above has a different printed spelling.
This completes the statement that the cup has circulated for the second time, the social example illustrating saifen.
Saihi is a hide, expressed by sai no kawa and Portuguese pele de bada. The dictionary retains the historical fi spelling in the compound headword.
Saihit is fine or detailed writing, glossed by komakana fude. The bare final t is retained as a historical checked ending rather than expanded to tçu.
The example saihit ni atawazu is translated below as having no need to write in detail. The scan restores t and n in Saifitni, where the draft misread mi.

runs.text: Não ha pera que eſcreuer miuda mente.

lines.note: The dictionary explains the formula as there being no need to write minutely. The separated miuda mente is retained, and the final usage label S. is upright.
Saihoo is the western direction, nishi no kata. Its downward caron is a graphic distinction from the circumflex in Saicô above.
Saihoo gokuraku names Amida's paradise in the west. The scan restores i and the downward caron in Saifǒ; Amida is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
The paradise is said to lie toward the west. The scan contains o between pera and poente, omitted from the draft; di- is completed here as dizem.
Saihoo joodo is given as equivalent to the western paradise described at the foot of column 1. The scan restores the missing accented o in Saifǒ; both printed o marks are downward carons.
Saihot means a recurrence, explained by futatabi okoru. The Portuguese begins with an illness returning; the final t and the nasal abbreviation in adoẽça are preserved.

runs.text: ferida, poſtema, ou chaga de pois deſtar bem.

lines.note: A wound, abscess, or sore can likewise return after improvement. The separated de pois and contracted deſtar retain the supplied historical wording.
Yamai, kizu nado saihot suru illustrates illness, wounds, and similar troubles recurring. The bare t before suru is not expanded to a modern syllabic spelling.
Saifuu or seifuu is the west wind, nishi no kaze. The scan supplies a downward caron on the first u as well as the second; the unusual Portuguese spacing O eſte is retained.
Saige is explained as mottomo shita, extremely low. This can describe low rank or quality as well as physical position.
Saige no hito applies the term to a very low or base person, clarifying the personal or social use of the adjective.
Saigen denotes an edge or limit, with kiwa and kagiri supplied as Japanese equivalents. It is distinct from the preceding word for lowness.
Saigen mo nai koto is something without a limit. The scan has an initial paragraph mark omitted from the draft; it is restored before the example.
The example is further described as immeasurable or immense, completing the negative construction saigen mo nai.
Saiget, glossed as toshitsuki, means years and months. The historical checked final t is retained in the headword.
Saiget wo heru means years and months passing. The final t of the noun remains before the attached object particle uo, rather than being converted to tçu.
This short continuation completes years and months in the time-passing example; it is not a separate entry.
Saigin is explained by futatabi ginzuru, repeating or chanting again. The Portuguese com continues as com-sigo in the physical lineation.

runs.text: ſigo algũa couſa como verſos, &c.em voz bai-

lines.note: The action is reciting verses or similar material to oneself in a low voice. The scan has the abbreviation &c.em, not the draft's &crem; baixa is divided at the edge.
The voice is low and intoned or chanted. Final S. is upright and marks written usage, outside the italic explanation.
Saigiri gives verb forms for anticipating or taking the initiative. Sai- begins the following example's saigitte.
Saigitte gojoo ni azzukaru describes receiving an honoured letter first. The Portuguese dã- begins the historical spelling of beforehand on the following row.

runs.text: temão de peßoa alta. i, Antes de eſcreuer pri-

lines.note: The letter comes from a person of high standing before the recipient has written first. The physical split pri- belongs to primeiro below.

The dictionary prefers Sayeguiru and directs the reader to its later entry. The word is embedded in the italic editorial apparatus. Enlargement confirms the small grave marks in Meliùs and infrà, which are retained.
Saijo is defined as a married woman. The printed molher is retained without modernizing its vowel.
Saigo is explained by shinuru toki, the moment of dying. The headword's final-time sense is illustrated in the following row.
Saigo ni oyobu means reaching one's final hour. The Portuguese à carries its printed grave accent, and initial v in voyobu is retained.
Sai-i is illustrated by sai-i daiichi no koto, something of outstanding eminence. The printed internal hyphen belongs to the Japanese form, not a physical line break.
This completes the definition as very eminent and excellent. The scan reads excelente with l, not the draft's excetente.
Saizen is given as equivalent to izen, before or previously. Saizen yori begins the example across the physical break.
Saizen yori moosu gotoku means as stated previously. The words remain joined as printed, rather than being segmented into modern grammatical units.
Saiji, equated with toki, names the time when Buddhist monks eat or take their meal. The specification of the monks follows below.
The definition concerns monks' meals, with upright S. marking written usage. Saiji ni han wo kissu illustrates taking food at that designated time; both long-s forms in qiſſu are retained.

runs.text: Comerem os Bonzos, ou jantarem a ſua hora,

lines.note: The Japanese example is translated as the monks eating or dining at their own appointed hour. The approximate time is given in the next row.
That hour is said to be near ten. The close-set daſdez, including its long s, is retained rather than silently normalized to separated modern words.
Saijin or saijinna is explained as a person of saikaku, ingenuity or resourcefulness. The alternative's initial long s and the nasal abbreviation in Homẽ are preserved.
The person has ingenuity and knowledge. A second application of saijinna hito begins, describing fluent speech below.
Saijinna hito can also mean a person who speaks well and readily. The tilde in expeditamẽte is retained without expanding it.
Saijoo means supremely excellent or highest. The source's long-o caron and superlative Portuguese wording are preserved.
Saijoo no on chiye illustrates supreme wisdom. Printed von chiye remains separated as in the scan, and sabedoria is divided at the right edge.
This completes sabedoria and gives saber as an alternative Portuguese expression for the supreme knowledge in the example.
Saimat means year's end, glossed by toshi no sue. The historical final t and the long s in ſuye are not modernized.

runs.text: Certa laya de pano de linho canemo crù

lines.note: Saimi names a kind of raw hemp or linen cloth. The Portuguese canemo and the grave in crù are retained as printed rather than replaced by modern spelling.

The cloth is used for katabira garments. Catabiras is a Japanese garment name embedded in Portuguese; enlargement supports retaining the local italic setting rather than imposing the more usual roman type for Japanese.

runs.text: Nome que ſe poem aos rapados, ou

lines.note: Saimin denotes a name given to tonsured people or monks. The defining feature of the name is supplied in the next row.

runs.text: Bonzos que ſe acaba em ſai. Vt,

lines.note: The name is said to end in sai. That suffix is embedded in Portuguese prose; Saimin- then begins the quoted question, with its printed line-end hyphen retained.
Saimin wa nanto moosu ka asks what the tonsured person's name is. Initial ua is retained as the dictionary's spelling of the particle, and the Portuguese question continues.
This completes the question about the name of a tonsured person. The question mark belongs to the printed translation, not to reviewer uncertainty.
Saimit is explained as komakani kibishii, minute and strict. The bare final t is important for understanding the form reused before ni below.
Saimit ni kyuume wo toguru describes carrying out a strict, exact examination. The damaged t-n sequence in Saimitni is read against the scan and the preceding headword, rather than the draft's mi.
The dictionary translates the example as judging with rigor and exactness. Ru completes toguru; final S. is an upright written-usage label.
